title: The Redundancy Effect
author: Jamie Clark
summary: This fourth edition of Jamie Clark's cognitive load theory series explains the redundancy effect, the cost students pay when they are given the same information twice. He separates it from split attention with one test: if students can understand a source on its own, the second source is redundant and should be cut, whereas if the two sources need each other they should be integrated. He supports the point with Chandler and Sweller's heart-diagram study, in which the diagram alone beat the diagram plus explanation, and with a meta-analysis showing that voice added to text students are already reading does not help on average, though it does help early readers and second-language readers. The edition lists five practical steps, including asking whether each element makes sense alone, keeping the clearest version, reading silently before explaining, putting key words rather than a script on the slide, and deciding what reading aloud is for. He closes with a worked example of stripping a World War One slide down to a diagram and three key words.
points: The redundancy effect applies when students can already understand one source, so the duplicate version consumes working memory without adding learning.
The test that separates it from split attention is whether a source makes sense alone: if not, integrate; if so, cut the repeat.
Reading slides aloud is not banned outright, because the evidence shows voice helps early readers and second-language learners while adding little for fluent readers.
Most fixes involve deleting, such as removing the paragraph under a clear diagram or trimming the slide to key words while the teacher explains.
Redundancy depends on prior knowledge, so an explanation a novice needs may become redundant as students gain security.
quotes: The redundancy effect is what happens when students are given information they don't need. Most often, that's the same information twice: words on a slide that we also say aloud, or a paragraph that describes a diagram students could already understand.
The students with the diagram alone learned more, in far less time. Writing the explanation onto the diagram didn't rescue it

Across 57 studies, adding the teacher's voice to text students were already reading didn't help on average. It did help students who were still learning to read fluently, and those reading in a second language.
So the real question is whether students need both versions at the same moment. Usually they don't, and the fix is simple: say it or show it, or do one and then the other.
The good news is that most redundancy can be fixed in a few minutes, usually by taking something away. The five steps below start with your resources and end with how you talk while students read.
If students need to read something, give them time to read it in silence before you talk about it.
If you change one thing this week, take your next slide with a full paragraph on it. Cut it to key words, or give students time to read it before you speak. Just don't do both at once.
